paragraphs.text: San He means Three Cranes, the [trademark](three-cranes:definition) of Wuzhou Tea Factory. The birds on it come from Hegang Tower, which stands beside the works. The factory opened for the export trade in 1953 and registered the [Three Cranes mark](san-he-liu-bao:three-cranes) in October 1991. This [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) comes from that same decade.

The factory has its own way of working the leaf. Since 1958 it has used [cold-water piling](san-he-liu-bao:cold-water-piling): workers moisten the leaves and heap them to ferment, and the method has been taught from one technician to the next on shift. After fermentation the tea rests in a [brick-and-timber warehouse](san-he-liu-bao:aging-warehouse), begun the year the factory opened, where porous wooden boards help keep moisture and temperature steady.

The shop records Guangzhou as one of the places this tea was stored. At thirty-one years it is well past the ten after which the trade counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged), and how it was kept matters as much as how long.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
